Noam Chomsky. An American linguist and cognitive scientist whose theory of generative grammar revolutionised linguistics in the nineteen fifties and sixties by proposing that humans possess an innate universal capacity for language. His work shifted the discipline from descriptive cataloguing toward the investigation of the mental structures underlying language, making him arguably the most influential linguist of the past century. He proposed that all human languages share a deep universal grammar—an innate mental system that constrains what languages can be. He introduced the concept of competence, the mental system underlying language, versus performance, what speakers actually do, refocusing linguistics on mental structures rather than observable utterances. He developed formal theories of syntax including phrase structure grammars and transformational grammar that model how humans generate and understand sentences. He demonstrated that simple descriptive methods, such as cataloguing sentence structures, cannot explain how finite rules generate infinite utterances—a central puzzle he solved through the principle of recursive generation. His work instigated a cognitive turn in linguistics and adjacent fields; he is equally famous as a political commentator and social critic whose ideas extend far beyond linguistics into philosophy, politics, and cognitive science, making him one of the most consequential public intellectuals of the modern era.
